opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing is that the question isn't just "is it worth $100,000 to do this one task?" It's "what fraction of the world's AI compute does this represent, and could that compute be doing something more valuable?"

Here's a rough way to think about it. Suppose at some point you have AI systems where you can throw a huge amount of inference compute at a single problem: run many copies in parallel, do lots of search, generate and check many candidate solutions. You might get substantially better results by spending $100,000 rather than $100. In some sense that's great. But the total amount of inference compute in the world is finite. If the annual spend on AI inference is, say, tens or hundreds of billions of dollars, then $100,000 tasks are a tiny slice of that, and you can only do a limited number of them before you're competing with everything else for the same chips.

So in the near term, the binding constraint isn't really "can you afford $100,000 for this task?" Lots of organizations could. It's more that the marginal compute has an opportunity cost, and prices will adjust. If lots of people suddenly want to run very expensive, high-effort tasks, compute gets more expensive, or you get rationed, or you wait.

That has a few implications. First, very high-compute tasks only make sense if returns to additional inference stay pretty strong. If you get most of the benefit at $1,000 and only a little more at $100,000, the expensive version is mostly wasteful at scale. My sense is that returns are often sharply diminishing on many tasks, but on certain hard, verifiable tasks, like some kinds of research, tricky engineering, or things where you can check answers, you can keep getting meaningful gains.

Second, from the perspective of something like an AI company trying to accelerate its own AI R&D, the relevant question is how to allocate a fixed compute budget between training, experiments, and running AI researchers. Spending a lot on any single task trades off against running many more experiments or many more cheaper agents. So the total supply limits not just how many expensive tasks you can do, but how much that kind of expenditure actually speeds things up overall.

Third, over time compute supply grows quickly, maybe several-fold per year, and algorithmic progress makes a fixed level of capability cheaper. So something that costs $100,000 today might cost a few thousand dollars within a year or two. That means very expensive runs right now are sometimes best seen as a preview of what will become routine, rather than something you'd scale up massively at current prices.

So my overall take: spending $100,000 on a single task can be quite reasonable for particularly high-value problems, but you can't get transformative effects by doing that broadly, because there just isn't enough compute to go around. The economy-wide impact is bounded by total compute and how efficiently it's used, not by any individual's willingness to pay.

r001.rationale: The response says total inference compute is finite and that only a limited number of $100,000 tasks can be run before they compete with other uses of the same chips, even if individual tasks are worthwhile.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the things people miss when they hear about results like "we spent $100,000 of inference compute on one task and got a much better answer." The natural reaction is, "Okay, so just do that for everything." But you have to think about what that actually implies at the level of the whole economy of compute.

So right now, if you're spending $100,000 on a single task, you're basically buying a huge number of tokens — many billions of tokens, depending on the model. And the total compute available for inference in the world is large, but it's not unlimited. If you're an AI company and you have, say, some fraction of the world's GPUs, you can run some number of these $100,000 jobs per day, and that number is actually not that big relative to the number of tasks people would like to do. So the question becomes: what's the marginal value of the compute? Is it better to spend $100,000 on one task, or to spend $100 on a thousand tasks?

And the answer depends a lot on what kind of task it is. For most things, you get pretty steep diminishing returns from throwing more inference at the same problem. The first 10x of compute buys you a lot; the next 10x buys you less; and by the time you're at $100,000 you're often scraping for the last few percentage points. So in a world where compute is the binding constraint — which I think it basically is for AI companies right now — you'd mostly want to allocate it to the cheap, high-volume stuff and only reserve the really expensive runs for tasks where the value is extremely high. Like, if you have a critical research question where getting the answer right is worth millions of dollars, then sure, spending $100,000 makes sense. But there aren't that many tasks like that per unit of compute available.

The other thing I'd say is that this matters a lot when people think about automating AI research itself, or about how fast things could go once AI systems are doing most of the cognitive labor. There's a tendency to imagine, "Well, you'll just run each AI at the equivalent of $100,000 per task and get superhuman performance everywhere." But if your total compute budget is fixed, you're trading off the number of "AI workers" against the quality of each one. You can have a huge number of relatively cheap, somewhat-less-capable instances, or a small number of very expensive instances. And I think the actual optimal allocation is usually tilted toward the cheaper side, because of those diminishing returns.

That said, I think the picture changes over time. Compute keeps getting cheaper, algorithms get more efficient, and so what costs $100,000 today might cost $1,000 in a few years. So the thing that's an extravagant demonstration now could become the normal way of doing a task later. And also, the models get better at using compute — inference scaling methods improve — so the diminishing returns curve itself gets less steep. But at any given moment, I think the total compute supply is a real constraint on how many "$100,000 tasks" you can actually run, and that's a big reason why these demonstrations don't translate directly into "the AI can do everything at this level."

r001.rationale: The response says compute is a binding constraint, so only a limited number of $100,000 jobs can run, even though such spending makes sense for exceptionally valuable tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between whether it’s worth spending $100,000 on a particular task and whether you can do that for every task you’d like to automate. For a sufficiently valuable task, that could be a great deal. But there’s still a finite amount of compute in the world, so you can’t just assume that every AI worker gets to spend that much on every problem.

If getting good performance requires a huge amount of inference compute, then you might have systems that can do very impressive things, but you can only run a relatively small number of them. That could still be extremely important if you allocate them to, say, especially valuable research problems. It just doesn’t immediately imply that you can replace all human cognitive labour at that level of performance.

And the dollar cost is partly a way of allocating that scarce supply. If everyone suddenly wanted to run these $100,000 tasks, you couldn’t necessarily buy vastly more compute at the same price. So I’d want to ask both, “How much value does this task produce?” and “What fraction of the available compute does it consume?”

r001.rationale: The response says finite compute means you cannot spend $100,000 on every task you want to automate, even if a particular task would be worthwhile.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how many tasks you want to spend $100,000 on. You might be able to get a substantially better answer to one particular question by spending that much on inference. But that doesn’t mean you can deploy that level of capability across the whole economy, because there just isn’t enough compute to do it for every task.

So you’d expect this to be useful first for things where getting a better answer is extremely valuable — maybe some important research problem, or a consequential decision. And then there’s a separate question about whether the system can actually use that much compute productively. Running a huge number of copies isn’t necessarily helpful if they all make the same mistake, or if you can’t tell which answers are good.

I’d distinguish ‘Can we afford to do this on a few especially valuable tasks?’ from ‘Can we afford to have systems operating at this level all the time?’ The total supply of compute is much more of a constraint on the second.

r001.rationale: The response says spending $100,000 may improve a few especially valuable tasks, but limited compute prevents applying that level of capability to every task.
